By eleven on Tuesday, Ada had finished everything on her list at the Toronto insurance office. The rest of the day stretched ahead like an empty road.
She refreshed the weather. She reorganised her desktop icons by colour. She read a long article about a lighthouse keeper, then another about sourdough. Each time she clicked something new, there was a tiny lift, then nothing.

"Forty-two," Ada said. Then, more honestly: "I finish my work by eleven. Is that bad?"
"It means they're wasting you. Ask for the claims-data project. Nobody's touched it."
Ada went back to her desk and, for the first time all week, opened her email to her manager.

Nilesh-sir pulled up a chair. "Maybe you're not bored of scanning. Maybe you're just empty. Take Monday and Tuesday off. Then we'll talk about the new indexing system."

Dear Jagdish-ji,
You said to write if I ever felt lost after college. I think I'm not lost, just idle.
I've been at the district statistics office for a year now. The work is fine, but I finish it by lunch. After that I read news, rearrange files, take long tea breaks and scroll through recipes I will never cook. I feel guilty the whole time, like I'm stealing the afternoon.
I've wondered if I'm lazy. But I'm not tired, and on Sundays I happily spend five hours on the village school survey I volunteer for. So it isn't energy that's missing. I think it's meaning, or maybe just difficulty.
Do you think I should ask for the census analysis unit, even though it's harder? Or is it foolish to want harder work?
I miss your seminars, where every question felt like a puzzle.
With respect,
Shalini

Saturday nets. Aadhya has struggled against the short ball all season; usually she gets frustrated, swings wildly, and checks her phone between turns.
Today I set the bowling machine just a little quicker than her comfort level, not so fast that she'd flinch. The first few she missed. Then she started adjusting her back foot, ball by ball.
She stayed in the net for forty minutes. Her phone lay in her kit bag the whole time; she didn't look once. Other girls called her for water, and she didn't hear.
Afterwards she sat on the grass, very quiet. She said, "My head feels clear. Like after a long sleep." She was calm in a way I haven't seen from her after a match.
Next week I'll raise the machine speed one step, only if today's level starts to feel easy.

Urmila is one of the sharpest students in the tutorial when we discuss ideas aloud. But whenever a problem sheet appears, she pushes it away before reading it. Today she said, "I'll fail this anyway. I've always been bad at maths." She had not looked at question one.

Thursday night
Tutorial again. I'm Jatin, the TA for second-year organic chemistry, and today I watched Ayesha close her notebook before I'd even finished writing the problem on the board.
"I can't do mechanisms," she said. "I never could." The thing is, I've seen her answers in the viva. She understands more than she thinks.
I felt frustrated, not with her, with how fast she gave up. So I tried something. I went over and asked her only to draw the first arrow, just the first one, where the electrons move.
She stared at me like I was mad. Then she drew it. Right.
"Now the second?" She drew that too, slower.
By the end she had half the mechanism, and she looked almost annoyed at herself for doing it. I'll try the same thing next week, one arrow at a time.

qa.a: Jatin asked her to draw only the first arrow, where the electrons move.

Harsha asked me today how work is. I said fine. I'm Jatin, and I say fine now to everything.
For a year I asked my manager for a transfer to the Pune office, for a proper desk, even for one Saturday off a month. I wrote emails. I asked in person. Nothing. Not even a no.
Somewhere around March I stopped asking. I just do the work and go home. I don't feel angry any more. I don't feel much at all, honestly. Food tastes the same. Weekends go by.
Harsha went quiet and then said, "This sounds heavier than fine. Will you talk to someone? A counsellor, properly?" I laughed it off.
But the flatness has been here for months, not days. I looked up the counsellor on our company's wellbeing page tonight and booked a slot for Wednesday. Harsha said he'd walk me there.

Francis had taught at the government primary school in Kolar for two years. In that time he had written to the block office six times: the roof leaked into Class 3, the toilet door had no latch, there were no chalk boxes. Not one reply.
By this winter, he had stopped writing. When the rain came in, he moved the children's mats to the dry side. When chalk ran out, he bought it himself. He didn't complain in the staffroom any more either.
His colleague Mehak noticed. "You used to argue with everyone. Now you just nod."
"What's the point?" he said. "Nothing changes." He said it without any feeling at all.
Mehak didn't let it go. "Francis, you've been like this for months. Will you talk to the counsellor at the district health centre? I'll come with you on Saturday."
He looked at her for a long time, then nodded.

The school garden club met on Wednesdays behind the science block. Ms Vinita handed each child a paper packet of seeds and said, "You choose where to plant. Sun or shade. Near the tap or far. Then we see what happens."
Rekha, nine, walked the whole garden twice. She picked a corner by the wall where the morning sun hit, and she decided to water every Monday and Wednesday herself.
In the second week, nothing. She frowned at the soil. In the third week, a tiny green loop pushed through. Rekha crouched so close her nose nearly touched it. "I did that," she said to nobody. "I picked the sunny spot."
Her friend's seeds, planted in deep shade, were slower. Rekha offered to help move them.
Ms Vinita wrote in her register: Rekha asked today if she could choose the next plant too.

qa.a: She picked a corner by the wall where the morning sun hit.

qa.a: She felt thrilled and proud, crouching close and saying "I did that", because she could see her choice had worked.

qa.q: Why does letting children choose where to plant help them?
qa.a: Making a choice and then seeing the result gives children evidence that their actions change things, which builds their sense that effort matters.

qa.a: Ms Vinita probably sees a child growing in confidence, eager to make the next choice herself.

I'm Kiran, Deepak's older sibling, and I watched this happen over the summer holidays, in the hottest week of May.
Deepak's bicycle chain kept slipping. Usually he'd bring it to Papa and wait. This time Papa was travelling, so Deepak just sat in the shade of the gate staring at the bike.

School counsellor's note — Pranav
Vaibhav, Class 11, came to see me on Monday. His parents told him last month that they are separating. He said, "Everything's falling apart and I can't do anything about it." He had stopped doing homework and wasn't sleeping well.
I didn't try to fix the situation. I gave him a sheet of paper with a line down the middle. On the left, things he can't control. He wrote: whether they separate, where Papa will live, the arguments.
On the right, things he can. He was slower here. Then he wrote: when I study, going to cricket practice, talking to Nani, telling my class teacher, eating dinner with Ma.
He looked at the right side for a long time. "It's a longer list than I thought," he said.
Plan: he will pick two items from the right side this week. We will meet again on Friday, and I have checked that his mother knows he is coming to see me.

qa.q: What did Vaibhav write on the side of things he can't control?
qa.a: He wrote whether they separate, where Papa will live and the arguments.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when he first came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He felt helpless and overwhelmed, saying everything was falling apart and he couldn't do anything about it.

qa.q: Why is the two-column list a useful step for Vaibhav?
qa.a: Separating what he can and cannot control shows him real actions still in his hands, like studying and talking to Nani, which restores some sense of power.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav's mother feel knowing he is seeing the counsellor?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and grateful that he has support at school during a hard time for the family.

grounding: It shows, through a counsellor's note, a teenager facing his parents' separation listing what he can and cannot control, and acting on the first list to regain a sense of power.

15 August, night
Papa lost his job two weeks ago. I'm Hemant, fifteen, and since then the house has been so quiet it hurts. Mummy counts things in the kitchen. Papa sits by the window.
I've been lying in bed every night feeling like a useless lump. Today Vijay chacha came over and saw my face. He took me to the terrace and said, "Write two lists. What you can change, and what you can't."
Can't: Papa's job. The money. Whether Mummy worries.
Can: Study for the board exam so that's one less worry. Help Mummy with dinner. Walk with Papa in the evening, if he wants. Talk to Vijay chacha when it gets heavy, instead of lying in bed.
The second list was longer than I expected. After dinner, I asked Papa if he wanted to walk. He looked surprised, then got his slippers.

qa.a: Hemant asked if Papa wanted to walk.

qa.a: Hemant had been feeling useless and helpless, lying in bed as the house went quiet after Papa lost the job.

qa.a: Writing what can and can't be changed showed Hemant real steps within reach, like studying, helping with dinner and talking to Vijay chacha, which eased the helpless feeling.

qa.a: Papa seems surprised and perhaps touched, getting his slippers, glad of the company during a hard time.
